title: 'Boring is not bad': CEO of Southeast Asia's largest bank pitches Singapore as a haven amid global turmoil
description: Tan Su Shan, chief executive officer of DBS Group Holdings Ltd., speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival in Singapore, on Nov. 12, 2025. Bloomberg
body: Tan Su Shan, chief executive officer of DBS Group Holdings Ltd., speaking at the Singapore Fintech Festival in Singapore, on Nov. 12, 2025. Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesSINGAPORE — Southeast Asia's biggest bank by assets is making a pitch to investors that Singapore and its businesses can help them navigate many of the uncertainties around the globe."I love it that the 'Little Red Dot' we all call home was open … predictable, and almost kind of boring," said CEO of DBS Group Tan Su Shan at the DBS Asia Future Forward conference in Singapore, referring to the city-state by one of its nicknames. "In this huge time of volatility, 'boring' is not bad, right?"The investing and business climate worldwide has been upended by everything from trade wars and El Niño-related weather issues to the Iran conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war. Singapore, with its AAA-rated debt, stable political environment and position at the heart of Asia, is seen by many as a bastion of stability. Tan said similar characteristics define DBS.DBS has "one of the safest credit ratings in the world," she told CNBC in an interview on the sidelines of the conference. Temasek, the state-owned global investment company that managed assets worth 518 billion Singapore dollars ($404 billion) as of March 31 and is seen as contributing to Singapore's fiscal stability, is DBS's biggest shareholder.DBS is also in a strong position to navigate the economic uncertainty around the world, Tan said."Trade and supply chains are all fragmented," she said. "If you need to diversify your upstream supply chain, just because you're worried about geopolitics, because you're worried about blockages, because you're worried about the war and the Strait of Hormuz, DBS is a partner to help you ... We can help our customers pivot from one market to another quite quickly."Tan also addressed management of a workforce in the age of artificial intelligence, and how to find people who have the right skills to navigate the technology."Humans intrinsically are nimble and agile ... I tell all my managers, hire for attitude – because you know you can't buy attitude, you can't train attitude."—CNBC's Ying Shan Lee contributed to this article.

schema.headline: 'Boring is not bad': CEO of Southeast Asia's largest bank pitches Singapore as a haven amid global turmoil

title: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict
description: A view of the Reduc (Duque de Caxias Refinery) which is back in full operation following the U.S. government's announcement of additional tariffs in R
body: A view of the Reduc (Duque de Caxias Refinery) which is back in full operation following the U.S. government's announcement of additional tariffs in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil on June 4, 2026. Fabio Teixeira | Anadolu | Getty ImagesOil prices fell Tuesday as investors weighed prospects of more Russian energy entering global markets, while concerns over the Saudi-Houthi conflict limited losses.Brent crude futures declined 1.48% to $105.05 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures fell 1.57% to $92.27. President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies, despite bipartisan criticism from U.S. lawmakers who warned the move could undermine sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconBrent and WTI prices so far this yearIn a Truth Social post, Trump said that the European Union had spent billions of dollars on Russian energy imports and insisted he had made the right decision for Americans. The agreement would allow Russia to supply diesel to U.S. and global markets for six months.Goldman Sachs said additional Russian diesel supplies were unlikely to significantly ease pressure on global fuel prices, estimating that an increase of 800,000 metric tons, equivalent to roughly 6 million barrels, would lower wholesale diesel prices in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Europe by just $1 to $2 a barrel. The bank underscored in a note published Monday that Russian refinery outages jumped by 3 million barrels per day from a year earlier, limiting Moscow's ability to ramp up production. Global diesel markets remain under significant strain, with U.S. inventories down 14% from a year earlier and visible stocks in China falling 11%, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank attributed the shortages to seven consecutive months of declining global diesel production, with seaborne exports falling by 1.4 million barrels per day, or 20%, year on year.Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen attacked King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday, leaving 12 people dead and more than 300 injured in a major escalation.— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Oil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict

title: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack
description: Beth Hammack, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, during a research conference at the Federal Reserve Bank
body: Beth Hammack, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, during a research conference at the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas in Dallas, Texas, US, on Friday, Oct. 31, 2025. Desiree Rios | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesCleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack indicated Monday that tighter monetary policy might be needed to bring down inflation and the central bank should make fast, incremental adjustments."When feasible, I generally think it's preferable to make smaller adjustments, and to do so relatively quickly, rather than to wait and risk needing a larger course correction," Hammack, a voting member of the Fed's policymaking committee, said in prepared remarks delivered during the National Association of Business Economics annual gathering."Considering all the inputs that factor into my reaction function, a restrictive monetary policy stance is appropriate to ensure a timely return to 2 percent inflation," Hammack added.Hammack's comments implied that more interest rate hikes could be on the horizon. Fed officials signaled in September meeting minutes that they could vote to raise rates again — but did not give a clear indication on when such a decision would come.The Fed last month voted to increase interest rates for the first time in three years.Traders priced in a more than 78% likelihood that the central bank keeps rates unchanged at its policy meeting later this month, according to CME's FedWatch tool. But they see a nearly 88% chance of a hike at the Fed's final meeting of the year in December.Sticky inflation poses challenges for consumers, businesses and monetary policymakers alike, Hammack said. The Cleveland Fed chief said that, with the "breadth" of current inflationary pressures, she expects it will take "some time" to get annual price growth down to the central bank's goal of 2%.The personal consumption expenditures price index came in at 3.4% year over year in August. The so-called core reading of the index, which strips out volatile food and energy costs and is favored by the Fed, registered at 3% compared with a year prior."Long-run inflation expectations have stayed remarkably well anchored despite actual inflation being above target for more than five years," Hammack said. "But I'm not taking that for granted.""With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy," she said.

schema.headline: Higher rates could be needed to avoid 'inflationary mindset' taking hold, says Fed's Hammack

title: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
description: US President Donald Trump and SpaceX Founder and CEO Elon Musk speak to the media at the White House driveway following a luncheon for tech leaders in
body: US President Donald Trump and SpaceX Founder and CEO Elon Musk speak to the media at the White House driveway following a luncheon for tech leaders in the East Room, in Washington, D.C., US, Sept. 29, 2026. Jonathan Ernst | ReutersElon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November.The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC.The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also gave more than $76 million to America PAC, the group he founded during the 2024 election, which has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races.The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election. The scale of the latest giving is historic: Musk's $158 million contribution to Senate Leadership Fund is among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history.The new figures were disclosed days ahead of a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline, when political committees are due to report their third-quarter finances.The Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas, where GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico. Talarico leads Paxton 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average as of Oct. 12.Musk separately gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Paxton. He also contributed $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Times reported and Curnutte confirmed.The trillionaire's footprint in Texas has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Tesla, X and The Boring Company now headquartered in the state and SpaceX growing its manufacturing and launch operations there.The political spending is also a sharp reversal from Musk's public comments last year."In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," Musk said in May 2025.At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump's administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship, appearing together at several recent events.Musk also retains deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month also named him co-director of Project Meridian, a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare.— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor

title: How Red Bull's F1 team is using AI to make split-second decisions for Max Verstappen
description: SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 11: Mechanics celebrate from the pit wall as Race winner Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red B
body: SINGAPORE, SINGAPORE - OCTOBER 11: Mechanics celebrate from the pit wall as Race winner Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains takes the chequered flag during the F1 Grand Prix of Singapore at Marina Bay Street Circuit on October 11, 2026 in Singapore, Singapore. (Photo by Peter Fox/Getty Images)Peter Fox | Getty Images Sport | Getty ImagesRed Bull Racing is now using artificial intelligence to help team staff make critical race-day decisions.Across Formula 1, tech giants are expanding their partnerships with racing teams as AI finds its way into everything from race strategy to fan engagement. Google is working with McLaren to integrate its Gemini AI tools, while Mercedes-AMG Petronas has partnered with Microsoft to use AI and cloud technology for performance analysis and race strategy. Ferrari, meanwhile, is working with IBM to develop AI-powered experiences for fans.Red Bull Racing and Oracle have developed an AI-powered strategy agent to help engineers interpret Formula 1 regulations and past rulings. Initially designed as a search tool, the system has evolved to recommend actions during races, Jack Harington, head of technical and performance partnerships at Oracle Red Bull Racing, told CNBC in an interview.Initially a search tool, the system has evolved into an agentic AI that draws on a wider range of information sources, Harington said."It's actually making decisions for us," he added. As an example, Harington pointed to the 2025 Italian Grand Prix in Monza, when Max Verstappen cut a corner while defending his position. The AI agent recommended that Red Bull give back the position to avoid a potential penalty, he added. While that went against the team's competitive instincts, Red Bull followed the advice, and Verstappen subsequently overtook his rival, Harington said.Still, Harington stressed that humans remain involved in the decision-making process."Formula One is and will always be a human sport," he said. He does not see AI completely replacing engineers and strategists, but rather enhancing their capabilities and allowing them to focus on their strengths, noting that there are "so many different variables" in Formula 1, from what happens on and off the track to the broader championship picture.The team also had reason to celebrate on the track Sunday, as Max Verstappen claimed his first-ever Singapore Grand Prix victory, taking his career win tally to 73.

schema.headline: How Red Bull's F1 team is using AI to make split-second decisions for Max Verstappen

title: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street chip sell-off
description: The SK Hynix Inc. booth at the Computex 2026 expo in Taipei, Taiwan, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. Lam Yik Fei | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsian technology
body: The SK Hynix Inc. booth at the Computex 2026 expo in Taipei, Taiwan, on Tuesday, June 2, 2026. Lam Yik Fei | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAsian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment.Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.9% — both hit their lowest intra-day levels since August.In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.03%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.6%, while Advantest, which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.38%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.76%, Disco lost 4.83% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.89%.The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, which reported progress on a new chip structure.Over the weekend, CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space."Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling."In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email.CXMT shares were down over 2%.'Vulnerable' AI sentiment?Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers, demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected.But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share."More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said.He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape."I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power.The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.

schema.headline: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street chip sell-off

title: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation
description: watch nowStarbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover."Starbuck
body: watch nowStarbucks on Monday denied it is considering acquiring Chipotle Mexican Grill in what would be the biggest-ever restaurant takeover."Starbucks is not buying Chipotle," a Starbucks spokesperson told CNBC's Jim Cramer. Chipotle's stock was down nearly 4% in morning trading Monday following the statement, while Starbucks shares were 1% higher.The coffee giant's denial comes after days of rumors about a potential megadeal between the two restaurant companies. On Thursday, the Financial Times reported that Starbucks had been working with advisors on a Chipotle takeover proposal in recent months. The newspaper cited people familiar with the matter.Earlier in October, Semafor reported that Chipotle had hired advisors to defend against activist investors or an unwanted takeover bid. The fast-casual chain is trying to recover from a rocky 2025, when traffic to its restaurants fell. Chipotle shares are down about 20% over the last year, making it a cheaper target.The deal rumors sent shares of Chipotle higher, while Starbucks stock fell on the reports. Chipotle investors were looking forward to a potential reunion with Brian Niccol, who previously led Chipotle and is now CEO of Starbucks. But Starbucks shareholders were largely concerned about an expensive distraction while the coffee chain is in the middle of its own turnaround.

schema.headline: Starbucks says it is not buying Chipotle after takeover speculation

title: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
description: Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesIndia's he
body: Shoppers gather at New Market in Kolkata, India, on September 21, 2026, ahead of the Durga Puja festival. Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesIndia's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release.Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023, joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.Inflation risks mountIndia is among the countries most vulnerable to the supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%. The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino, with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs. The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

schema.headline: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates

title: Delta delays debut of Saudi Arabia service until March after Riyadh airport attacks
description: watch nowDelta Air Lines said it will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and the Saudi capital Riyadh until March after several d
body: watch nowDelta Air Lines said it will delay the launch of its nonstop service between Atlanta and the Saudi capital Riyadh until March after several deadly attacks hit the city's airport there.Delta planned to begin the route on Oct. 23, with an Airbus A350-900 wide-body plane, in what would have marked the first nonstop commercial flight between the U.S. and Saudi Arabia operated by a U.S. airline.Since Thursday, more than 2,000 flights have been canceled to and from King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to FlightAware. The deadly attacks, claimed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, escalated Saturday, when a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the airport, officials said, killing at least 12 people and wounding more than 300.King Khalid International Airport remains closed as of Monday."We remain in close contact with relevant government and aviation partners, including Saudia and Riyadh Air, as we monitor the situation," Delta said in a statement. "Saudi Arabia remains an important market for Delta, and we are committed to serving the Kingdom for the long-term."Delta CEO Ed Bastian had told CNBC on Thursday that the airline hadn't yet decided whether to postpone the debut. "Obviously, we were disappointed to see the news this week," he said. "Safety is going to make the call."Delta's decision came after the Federal Aviation Administration on Sunday issued a warning for U.S. airlines.The FAA said pilots should "exercise caution" in or around Saudi Arabia "due to safety-of-flight risks associated with ongoing military activities" and navigation systems. In the warning, which is in effect until Dec. 10, the agency said the threats could be a potential risk "to aircraft at all altitudes." Airlines suspended flights to the airport, some for the rest of the week, while countries including the U.S. and Australia advised citizens against travel to the region.— CNBC's Michele Luhn contributed to this report. title: Six Flags shares plunge after-hours following report of deadly roller coaster incident
description: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen.
body: UKRAINE - 2021/08/25: In this photo illustration the Six Flags Entertainment Corporation (Six Flags Theme Parks) logo is seen on a smartphone screen. (Photo Illustration by Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesShares of Six Flags Entertainment plunged more than 10% in after-hours trading Monday following reports of a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia, marking a sharp reversal from gains during the regular session. The stock had closed 4.5% higher during regular trading before the after-hours sell-off.One person died and several others were injured in an incident involving the park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County shortly before 4 p.m. Monday, according to the report, citing local police.Police did not provide additional details about the incident, the report showed. Witnesses told a local news station they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, the report said. Six Flags said its park staff and local authorities responded immediately to the incident, adding that it was cooperating fully with the investigation, had temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks and would not release further details out of respect for the family's privacy, according to the report.The company's shares have fallen 22% year to date.

schema.headline: Six Flags shares plunge after-hours following report of deadly roller coaster incident

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'
description: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington
body: Representative Ilhan Omar, a Democrat from Minnesota, during a news conference ahead of the State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. Daniel Heuer | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFederal authorities raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday morning as part of a criminal investigation of the Minnesota Democrat. Omar, who has not been charged with a crime, said she was being targeted for political purposes because of her opposition to President Donald Trump.A person familiar with the situation, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublic investigation, told CNBC that the probe of the 44-year-old congresswoman is complex and has been going on for years.MS NOW reported that a law enforcement source with direct knowledge of the raid — which comes weeks before November's midterm election — said the investigation into Omar is based on allegations of fraud.Fox News, which first reported the raid, cited a source familiar with the probe as saying it is focused on her immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her father when she emigrated to the U.S. with him from Somalia as a child. Homeland Security Investigations, a division of the Department of Homeland Security, conducted the raid. HSI investigators were seen outside Omar's home in the Northeast quadrant of Washington throughout the morning.Omar, who is seeking reelection, has been a target of criticism by Trump for years. She heckled the president during his State of the Union address to Congress on Feb. 24, which came on the heels of aggressive immigration enforcement actions in Minneapolis by federal authorities.Omar, who is deputy chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, blasted the raid and the investigation in a post on X on Monday.Homeland Security Investigations Police remove documents from the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-MN) on Oct. 12, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Leyden | Getty Images"I'm ok," Omar wrote. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she wrote."I will not be silenced."Omar became a U.S. citizen in 2000 at 17. She was elected to Congress in November 2018 to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis.She and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., became the first two Muslim women elected to Congress.The Department of Justice, in a statement to CNBC when asked about the raid, said, "Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.""This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," the DOJ said.Omar's spokeswoman, Jacklyn Rogers, in a statement said, "This raid by Trump's DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies.""For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," Rogers said. "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told right-wing commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas that DHS was investigating issues around Omar and her family's immigration to the United States."There may be more to this, the whole family migration and possibly some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with," said Mullin. He said the investigation could end with deportations.The DOJ, for years, has had a policy regarding the announcement and initiation of federal investigations and prosecutions close to elections. The policy discourages beginning an investigation, taking investigative steps, bringing criminal charges, or making public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or to give a candidate an advantage or disadvantage.The person familiar with the raid on Omar's home told CNBC on Monday that the DOJ does not consider that action to violate the policy because the raid was not meant to be public.Republican John Nagel is running against Omar in a race the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter rates "solid Democrat." The general election is just over three weeks away on Nov. 3.The Democratic leadership of the House of Representatives blasted the Trump administration for the raid."The Trump administration's raid on Congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home is deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump's adversaries," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., Minority Whip Katherine Clark, D-Mass., and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, the Democratic Caucus chair, in a statement."For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations," the statement said. "Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family.""The American people deserve transparency, and we will deliver full accountability for the rogue abuse of power from the Department of Homeland Security and Department of Justice."

schema.headline: Rep. Ilhan Omar blasts federal criminal raid on home: 'I will not be silenced'

title: Earnings beats are now the norm. What the stock market needs to keep rallying
description: Goldman Sachs signage on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty
body: Goldman Sachs signage on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Tuesday, July 14, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesWill 30% profit growth and upbeat tech guidance be enough to keep the rally going? We'll soon find out.  Third-quarter earnings season kicks into gear Tuesday with JPMorgan Chase and other big banks. Expectations are steep: consensus forecasts call for nearly 30% year-over-year growth, according to FactSet. That's up from around 27% three months ago. But 30% or more should be doable — S&P 500 profits have topped quarterly estimates by healthy margins since mid-2023.  Tech will have to do its part at beating estimates and lifting guidance. For now, the sector shows no signs of slowing. Analysts expect 65% gains for tech profits, up from an estimated 57% growth three months ago. Upward revisions for Nvidia, Micron Technology and Dell Technologies are doing the heavy lifting, according to FactSet.Also positive, profit growth is broadening beyond the Mag 7. The other 493 stocks in the S&P 500 are forecast to deliver 27% year-over-year gains, topping the Mag-7 average, according to Russell Investments. S&P 400 MidCap operating earnings should rise 19% in 2026, notes Ed Yardeni, head of Yardeni Research. Banks first at batThe first earnings test comes with the big banks. JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, reporting Tuesday, should reveal how steeper interest rates are impacting loan growth, balance sheets, M&A activity and the IPO pipeline. JPMorgan — the largest U.S. bank — will be critical, along with comments from CEO Jamie Dimon who tends to move markets with his outlook.Financials are on a knife's edge; the sector is hovering around its 200-day moving average, a key technical indicator, after falling 5% since August 31. Analysts see rising interest rates starting to sting loan growth and fixed-income securities held on balance sheets. The weakness could make for a relief rally, but earnings and guidance could go either way, pushing the stocks up or down, notes Julian Emanuel, senior managing director at Evercore ISI. "There will be volatility as investors hang on every word from the Big Banks this week," he said in a note.Emanuel remains bullish on the market, however, and tech in particular. Several other strategists concur.Goldman Sachs shifted to an "overweight" stance on equities Monday, saying "growth remains supportive." The bank's strategists see a favorable macro climate with low recession risk. And they expect inflation to ease in 2027 — all of which points to "more of a 'Goldilocks' backdrop," according to a note by Christian Mueller-Glissmann, head of asset allocation at Goldman Sachs Research.For positioning, he recommends a "barbell of AI beneficiaries and selective rate-sensitive, high-dividend and low-volatility stocks that could benefit from eventual rate relief."The setup also looks favorable because multiples have fallen, notes Lisa Shalett, chief investment officer for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management. Stocks are trading at 19 times forward earnings, down from 21 times over the summer, despite the fact that earnings growth has picked up. While rising bond yields have compressed multiples, "that's typical of a midcycle expansion when rate hikes have yet to truly bite," she points out.Shalett also takes solace in the market's growth drivers. "While many sectors will likely eventually be impacted by higher-for-longer rates, the key growth vectors for this boom — AI capex and wealth-linked consumption — have thus far proved rate-insensitive," she said in a note Monday. UBS sees gains for equities too. "Investors should remain positioned for market upside, and we forecast the S&P 500 to reach 8,400 by June next year," said Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and Global Head of Equities for UBS Chief Investment Office in a recent note.More critical than bank earnings may be tech — a sector accounting for 40% of the S&P 500 and about a third of its estimated $800 billion in profits this quarter. Analysts will be looking for signals that AI chip and infrastructure demand are powering through a tough macro climate and higher energy prices, and the stocks will move on 2027 guidance.The first clues may come when Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company reports Thursday. Third-quarter profit estimates for TSM are up to $4.45 a share, from $3.42 in January, according to FactSet consensus forecasts. TSM has beaten forecasts in 19 of the last 20 quarters, including a 10.8% beat in the second quarter. Its outlook on chip demand will be a key indicator for Nvidia and other chipmakers.The Nasdaq 100 is sitting near record highs, however, thanks to a swath of AI companies issuing upbeat reports and new products — easing some of the consternation about the cycle topping out. Micron delivered a knockout quarter. On the consumer side, Meta Platforms' launch of its Muse agent has set off an arms race to capture AI-enabled consumer e-commerce, while also catapulting its stock. Trouble below the surface?Granted, the market's reliance on tech belies weakness elsewhere. Of the 504 stocks in the S&P 500, nearly 38% are off 20% or more from their 52-week high. It's a mark of narrow breadth as investors reward a few hot sectors (primarily tech and energy) while others languish. Earnings revisions have also turned negative in many cases. Eight sectors have seen negative revisions in bottom-up EPS estimates since June 30, led by materials (-10.2%), consumer staples (-4%) and health care (-3.3%), according to FactSet. Also of note, earnings will be a test for the market's multiple. While the S&P 500's P/E has dropped to about 19 times, the index "reads expensive" on 17 of 20 valuation measures, according to Bank of America, adding that implies a -3% annualized return over the next decade.BofA does see a positive setup for the quarter, expecting 32% earnings growth, a roughly 3% beat to consensus. But after two quarters of companies blowing past forecasts, "healthy beats are the status quo and may not be enough to drive stocks higher," BofA says. It may also take more than a healthy AI outlook to keep the rally going. As BofA notes, "the interplay between geopolitics, rates and Tech may be underestimated — a higher cost of capital and geopolitical bottlenecks could gum up what has so far been a mostly smooth story."Something to chew on as markets start digesting third-quarter results.

schema.headline: Earnings beats are now the norm. What the stock market needs to keep rallying

title: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'
description: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn on October 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. Aaro
body: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to members of the media as he departs the White House on the South Lawn on October 10, 2026 in Washington, DC. Aaron Schwartz | Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump on Monday defended last week's decision to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian diesel fuel exports after the announcement drew bipartisan criticism.Trump, in a Truth Social post, accused the media of hypocrisy for allegedly refusing to cover past purchases of Russian energy by the European Union."The European Union paid Russia 250 Billion Dollars for Energy, and the Fake News Media doesn't want to get near that story," Trump wrote. While the president did not specify, his figure roughly tracks with some estimates of how much the EU has spent importing fossil fuels from Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The European Commission has launched a plan to phase out its dependence on Russian energy. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!" Trump wrote in the social media post.Lawmakers from both parties raised concerns about Trump's decision to let Russia supply some diesel to the U.S. and global markets for the next six months. The plan received pushback from multiple congressional Republicans who have urged Trump not to lift the U.S. ban on energy imports from Russia until its president, Vladimir Putin, ends the war against Ukraine."The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," a group of seven senators, including four Republicans, said in a joint statement on Sunday.Other Republicans have also raised issues with Trump's deal."While I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said Friday.Trump, whose party is staring down a potentially tough midterm election that has coincided with widespread economic dissatisfaction, says the plan he coordinated with Putin will help bring down sky-high diesel prices. Some analysts say the policy won't make much of a dent, however.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."

schema.headline: Trump defends Russia diesel deal after bipartisan pushback: 'I made the right choice'

title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
description: A Microsoft Azure Maia 300 prototype chip.MicrosoftMicrosoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance o
body: A Microsoft Azure Maia 300 prototype chip.MicrosoftMicrosoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack. Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon, Advanced Micro Devices, Cerebras, Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD. Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade."Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models.Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline."We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said.Read more CNBC tech newsAI's quiet safety gatekeepers are stepping into the spotlightMicrosoft's Nadella says AI needs an 'emergency brake' that humans controlNvidia GPUs are everywhere. Here are the ways companies are accessing themHollywood takes on Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman amid widespread anxiety over AIMicrosoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs."We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have,"  Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well."Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies."Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI tradewatch now

title: GM CEO: We're making leaps and bounds toward 'eyes-off, hands-off' driving
description: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Oct 12 20266:40 PM EDTUpdated 4 Hours AgoKey PointsGeneral Motors CEO Mary Barra said the au
body: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Oct 12 20266:40 PM EDTUpdated 4 Hours AgoKey PointsGeneral Motors CEO Mary Barra said the automaker is still on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028, starting with the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ.After exiting its Cruise robotaxi business, GM is focusing on autonomous technology for personal vehicles.watch nowGeneral Motors CEO Mary Barra said Monday that the automaker remains on track to introduce "eyes-off, hands-off" driving technology by 2028.GM announced last October that it plans to launch its next-generation driver-assistance system in the electric Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028 before expanding to other models. Unlike the company's existing Super Cruise system, which allows drivers to take their hands off the wheel but requires them to remain attentive, the new technology is designed to let drivers take their eyes off the road under certain conditions.Barra told CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money" that she recently tested the technology and was impressed by how much it had improved since an earlier ride in March. "They're making so much progress on our goal to have eyes off, hands off in the '28 time frame," the CEO said. "We're going to be well positioned from a personal autonomy perspective." She added, "When people want to drive, they can. When they don't, they won't need to as that grows."GM's push into personal autonomous driving follows its decision to exit its Cruise robotaxi business in December 2024 after spending more than $10 billion. Rather than compete in the increasingly crowded driverless ride-hailing market, the automaker redirected its resources toward developing autonomous systems for vehicles consumers own. "We're not in the taxi business. We're not in the bus business," Barra said. She acknowledged that exiting the robotaxi market was difficult but defended the move, noting that GM retained much of the Cruise team to work on personal autonomous driving. "It was a tough decision, but I think it was the right decision," she said. Barra also pushed back against the idea that widespread adoption of autonomous vehicles could eventually reduce the need for personal car ownership. She recalled earlier predictions that ride-hailing services such as Uber and Lyft would sharply reduce vehicle sales, something that never materialized because "people still value that it's in my driveway. I can go wherever I want, whenever I want." watch now

schema.headline: GM CEO: We're making leaps and bounds toward 'eyes-off, hands-off' driving
